slides.label: Title
slides.narration: Open with Klein's Erlangen program: geometry is the study of properties invariant under a group of transformations. Different groups define different geometries, and the hierarchy of groups organizes the four pillars into a single framework. Orient students to printed pages 143 through 173.

slides.label: Lecture Route
slides.narration: Preview the five themes. Students should leave understanding the hierarchy of transformation groups from isometries to projective maps, the role of quaternions in representing rotations, spherical geometry as the geometry of the rotation group, finite rotation groups and their classification, and the connection between S3 and RP3.

slides.label: Group Hierarchy
slides.narration: Present the hierarchy of transformation groups. Isometries preserve distance and are the transformations of Euclidean geometry. Affine maps preserve parallelism and ratios but not distance. Projective maps preserve only incidence and cross-ratio.

slides.label: Spherical Geometry
slides.narration: Introduce spherical geometry as the geometry of the unit sphere with its intrinsic metric. Great circles are the geodesics and they always intersect, so there are no parallel lines. The angle sum of a spherical triangle exceeds 180 degrees by the area.

slides.label: Quaternions
slides.narration: Present quaternions as a four-dimensional extension of complex numbers used to represent rotations in three dimensions. A unit quaternion q acts on a vector v by conjugation: v maps to qvq inverse. This avoids gimbal lock.

slides.label: Finite Rotation Groups
slides.narration: Classify the finite rotation groups of three-space: cyclic groups, dihedral groups, and the three exceptional Platonic groups (tetrahedral, octahedral, icosahedral). There are no other finite subgroups of SO(3).

slides.label: SO(3) and RP3
slides.narration: Present S3 as the space of unit quaternions and show that SO(3) is the quotient S3 divided by the identification q equals minus q. This gives RP3, connecting topology, algebra, and geometry.

slides.label: Recap
slides.narration: Summarize the chapter by connecting the transformation hierarchy, quaternions, spherical geometry, finite rotation groups, and the topology of SO(3) into Klein's program. The properties that matter in each geometry are exactly those preserved by the corresponding transformation group.
